extracted.intended_audience: readers and practitioners of literary criticism; educated general readers; writers
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative guidance and exemplars for judging literary style, critical method, biography and diary-writing, as illustrated by remarks on Samuel Johnson and Madame D’Arblay. Emphasises natural speech, critical rigor, and the dangers of mannerism and parochial standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency in scepticism/credulity
rubrics_metrics.description: Be consistent in critical credulity: avoid being hyper-sceptical about ordinary oddities but credulous about miraculous tales. (Text: "He began to be credulous precisely at the point where the most credulous people begin to sceptical.")
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate evidence uniformly: rejecting unauthenticated anecdotes while granting respectful hearing to predictions, dreams, or ghost stories is inconsistent. Examples: Johnson rejects reports of water-spouts or meteoric stones but listens courteously to tales of second sight or accomplished dreams; anti-pattern is relaxing severity at the point where scepticism should increase.

rubrics_metrics.name: Severity in sifting evidence for odd claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply extreme severity when examining evidence for merely odd or extraordinary claims. (Text: "Johnson was in the habit of sifting with extreme severity the evidence for all stories which were merely odd.")
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demand robust testimony and corroboration for unusual assertions; do not allow intellectual laziness or sentimental bias to substitute for evidence. Note the anti-pattern where severity 'relaxed' for miraculous stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground criticism on sound premises, not mere precedent
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism should not 'rest on pure assumption' or only on precedent or authority; critics must give reasons 'drawn from the nature of things.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a work, state and defend foundational premises rather than assuming contemporary standards or appealing only to prior authorities. The author criticises Johnson for quoting precedent or authority without justifying the underlying assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid judging by parochial contemporary standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not take the tastes of your own age as the universal standard: avoid assuming "the kind of poetry which flourished in his own time... was the best kind of poetry."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise diversity of aesthetic principles across times and cultures; avoid automatic preference for works that conform to the critic's familiar contemporary norms (example: Johnson's preference for Pope's aesthetics leads to unfair assessments of Homer, old ballads, and newer novels).

rubrics_metrics.name: Write as one talks: favour natural, conversational expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer the natural idiom of speech in writing; 'If he had been content to write as he talked, he might have left books on the practical art of living superior to the Directions to Servants.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Valorise simple, energetic, picturesque expressions that resemble spoken language. Example contrast: Madame D’Arblay’s early diary ('true woman's English, clear, natural, and lively') versus later overwritten memoirs; Boswell/Johnson letters vs Johnson's published 'Johnsonese' style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mannerism adopted on principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Mannerism is tolerable or even admirable when it is natural, but 'a mannerism which does not sit easy on the mannerist, which has been adopted on principle... is always offensive.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If stylistic quirks feel forced or require constant effort, they will repel readers. By contrast, natural mannerisms (Milton, Burke) can be preserved. Assess whether an author's distinctive devices seem organic or affectation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer strong plain words over Latinate/Greek affectation
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Anglo-Saxon or Norman-French 'strong plain words' rather than gratuitous Greek and Latin borrowings: Johnson 'made less use than any other eminent writer of those strong plain words... and felt a vicious partiality for terms... borrowed from the Greek and Latin.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate diction for rootedness in the living language; excessive classicalism or learned affectation weakens clarity and naturalness. Anti-patterns: 'big words wasted on little things.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid padding with useless epithets and gratuitous antithesis
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not 'pad out a sentence with useless epithets' or employ antithetical forms where there is no real opposition; such padding makes prose stiff and unnatural.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for concise, necessary modifiers and meaningful contrast. Example faults listed: useless epithets, constant antithetical forms, 'big words wasted on little things.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid harsh inversions that distort natural syntax
rubrics_metrics.description: Refrain from 'harsh inversions so widely different from those graceful and easy inversions which give variety... to the expression of our great old writers.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use inversion sparingly and where it enhances rhythm or meaning; forced inversions create stiffness and draw negative attention to style rather than content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personation/voice: characters should speak distinctively
rubrics_metrics.description: Successful personation requires distinct voices for characters; failure is 'No man surely ever had so little talent for personation as Johnson... he wrote in the same pompous and unbending style.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate narrative dialogue and characterisation for authenticity and variety of voice. Anti-pattern: identical elevated diction across different characters or types (e.g., fops, coquettes, poets) that destroys illusion of persona.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve original simplicity when translating/adapting speech
rubrics_metrics.description: When converting letters or spoken material into published form, preserve the original simplicity and force (example: letters from the Hebrides are the 'original' and Journey is the 'translation').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare source (private speech/letters) with published version: avoid over-ornamenting or 'translating' simple speech into an unnatural literary dialect ('Johnsonese').

rubrics_metrics.name: Diary-writing: favour early clear, natural, lively manner over later overwrought rhetoric
rubrics_metrics.description: The Diary of Madame D’Arblay is praised as 'for the most part, written in her earliest and best manner, in true woman's English, clear, natural, and lively' while later Memoirs display a 'peculiar rhetoric' that deforms the pages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In evaluating personal prose (diaries, memoirs), value immediacy, clarity and natural diction; beware of later stylistic mannerisms that make reading laborious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broaden critical perspective beyond local experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid limiting generalisations based only on narrow social experience—'he had studied, not the genus man, but the species Londoner.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the writer's maxims and generalisations stand up beyond their immediate milieu. A critic or author who knows only a particular class/place risks drawing false universal conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use travel and history to prevent contraction of mind
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'real use of travelling and of studying history is to preserve men from the contraction of mind... to keep men from being what Tom Dawson was in fiction, and Samuel Johnson in reality.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value sources of broadening experience—travel, history, conversation—as tools for writers and critics to avoid narrow induction and confusing exceptions with rules. Anti-pattern: dismissing travelling/history as trivial ('What does a man learn by travelling?').

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge works on their appropriate kind and depth
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognise that a critic may be 'an excellent judge of compositions fashioned on his own principles' but fail when greater philosophical depth is required; do not overreach beyond one's critical competence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the critic's standards match the nature of the work under review. A critic skilled at judging conventional forms may misjudge original or philosophically deep works (example: Johnson's failings on Shakespeare and Milton).
